1. **The idea:** The image compares buying with renting using past US data. Each square in the grid is a start month between January 1991 and July 2016. A light square means the buyer came out ahead after ten years. A dark square means the renter came out ahead. The title says the buyer was ahead in about 3 of 4 cases (75.6%). A later label says the renter was ahead in 75 of 307 cases. The sources named are FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. The "ILLUSTRATIVE" badge and the note "US only · history, not a forecast" are both on screen.

2. **What changes:** The grid and the headline stay the same throughout. Frame 1 has only the buyer-ahead headline. Frame 2 shows the same grid with some of the dark squares dimmed or shifted. In frames 3 to 6 a "renter ahead: 75 of 307" label appears and the dark squares are highlighted. In frames 5 and 6 a caption is added at the bottom: "counted: interest · tax · insurance · repairs · buying and selling". The dark squares form a cluster in the middle of the timeline, with a few light gaps in it.

3. **What it means:** In this history, a buyer who counted all the costs, including interest, tax, insurance, repairs and the costs of buying and selling, usually came out ahead after ten years. Renting came out ahead in roughly a quarter of the start months. Those months are concentrated in one stretch, which I can't date from the image. So renting did not always cost more, but buying usually won.

4. **Advice:** The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer might take away that buying has usually paid off over a ten-year horizon, but that is an inference. The on-screen text warns that this is "history, not a forecast" and is limited to the US.

5. **Source of the conclusion:** The animation suggested the main finding, through the headline "buyer ahead: about 3 in 4" and the cost caption. It did not suggest any advice. Any advice, such as "buying is usually better," would be my own conclusion, and the "history, not a forecast" label cautions against drawing it.
